title: Downward Paths That Add Up
statement:
You get the root of a binary tree of integers and a number target. Count the paths whose values add up to exactly target.

A path is a chain of one or more nodes where each next node is a child of the previous one. It may start at any node and stop at any node below it, but it can never go back up or jump across to a sibling.

Trees are written in level order with null for a missing child. An empty tree has no paths.

examples.why: 2 → 1 → 2, then 2 → 3, and the single node 5. A path does not need to start at the root or end at a leaf.
The node 2, the leaf 2, −3 → 5 and 3 → −1. Negative values mean you cannot stop extending a path once the sum passes the target.
1 → −1, 1 → −1 → 0, and the single 0. Adding a zero to a matching path gives another matching path.

hints: Fix where a path ends. Every path is then a suffix of the root-to-node chain above that end. How do you count suffixes with a given sum?
Keep the running sum from the root down to the current node. A suffix ending here adds up to target exactly when an earlier prefix sum equals running − target.
Walk the tree depth-first with a hash map counting the prefix sums on the current root-to-node chain only. Add the current sum on the way down and remove it on the way back up.

explain.intuition:
Any downward path sits on one root-to-node chain. On that chain, the sum of a stretch is the difference of two prefix sums: the running sum at its bottom minus the running sum just above its top. So the question "how many paths end at this node with sum target" becomes "how many ancestors' prefix sums equal running − target". That is the same trick as counting subarrays with a given sum, applied to the chain you are standing on.

A hash map of prefix sums answers that in O(1). The catch is that the map must only hold sums from the current chain, so a node in one branch never pairs with a node in another. Add the sum when you enter a node and remove it when you leave, like pushing and popping a breadcrumb trail.
steps: Start the map with {0: 1}: an empty prefix, so paths that start at the root are counted.
Visit a node: running += node.val, then add map[running − target] to the answer.
Increment map[running] and recurse into both children.
On the way back up, decrement map[running] so siblings and other branches do not see it.
pitfalls: Stopping a path as soon as its sum exceeds the target. Values can be negative, so a later node can bring it back down.
Forgetting the {0: 1} seed. Paths that start at the root are then never counted.
Not removing a prefix sum after finishing a node. Then a path could seem to run from one subtree into its sibling.

complexity.space: O(h) for the map and the recursion, where h is the height

solutions.title: Start a downward walk from every node
solutions.idea: For each node, walk every path going down from it and count the ones that hit the target.
solutions.time: O(n · h), O(n²) on a chain

solutions.title: Prefix sums on the current chain
solutions.idea: Count earlier prefix sums equal to running − target with a hash map that only holds the current root-to-node chain.

followups: Return the paths themselves instead of the count. How does the output size change the complexity?
Paths may now also bend once at a node (go up from one child, down into the other). What changes?
